office.title: Indiana County Sheriff
office.summary: The sheriff is an elected county officer created by the Indiana Constitution who arrests offenders, keeps the peace, serves court papers, keeps order in county courts and runs the county jail [1, 2]. The Indiana Sheriffs' Association describes sheriffs as constitutional officers elected by the people, whose work includes operating jails, serving civil process, providing court security and coordinating emergency response [3]. Every county elects its sheriff in 2026 for a four-year term, and no one may serve as sheriff more than eight years in any twelve-year period [1].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years; the sheriff serves until a successor is elected and qualified [4, 1]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: Countywide by the county's voters on the partisan general election ballot; all county sheriffs are elected in 2026 [1]

facts.label: Term limit
facts.value: No more than eight years in any period of twelve years (Indiana Constitution, Article 6, Section 2) [1]

facts.label: Qualifications
facts.value: Must have lived in the county for at least one year before the election, be registered to vote in the county by the filing deadline, and file a statement of economic interests; a sheriff who moves out of the county forfeits the office [1, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: A county may pay the sheriff a salary from the county general fund of at least 50% to 100% of the state minimum salary of a full-time prosecuting attorney, depending on county population [5]

duties: Arrests without a warrant people who commit an offense in the sheriff's view, brings them before a county court, and holds them while the arrest is investigated [2].
Suppresses breaches of the peace and pursues and jails felons [2].
Takes care of the county jail and the prisoners held there [2, 3].
Serves and carries out legal papers (process) directed to the sheriff by courts and the county commissioners [2].
Attends and keeps order in all courts of the county, which the Sheriffs' Association describes as providing court security [2, 3].
Takes photographs, fingerprints and other identification data from people held for crimes, and DNA samples for felonies [2].
Reports twice a year to the Indiana Department of Correction the average daily cost of holding a jail prisoner [2].
Holds state prisoners, including people convicted of Level 6 felonies, in the county jail, for which the state reimburses counties at a daily rate set in the state budget [7].
Coordinates emergency response and works with local police, prosecutors and community partners [3].

In a county whose council creates a sheriff's merit board by ordinance, appoints three of its five members, while the county police officers elect the other two; no more than two sheriff appointees and one elected member may belong to the same party [8].

Must report information to federal authorities when a person arrested for a felony or misdemeanor is believed to lack legal immigration status, and, since July 2026, notify the judge setting bail when holding a person subject to an immigration detainer [9, 10].
May supervise and inspect businesses such as pawnbrokers and secondhand dealers [2].

What the sheriff does not control: the county commissioners must establish and maintain the county jail building [11]; the county makes the appropriation for feeding prisoners and sets the sheriff's salary [5]; the prosecuting attorney decides which crimes to prosecute [12]; and judges decide bail [13].
recent_changes: February 2025: The Indiana Department of Correction said funding to reimburse county jails for holding Level 6 felons and state prisoners, then $40 per day, was exhausted for state fiscal year 2025; Tippecanoe County Sheriff Robert Goldsmith, then president of the Indiana Sheriffs' Association, called it very disappointing, and Rep. Greg Steuerwald (R-Avon) said everything owed would be paid [14].

2025: The new state budget raised the daily rate for Level 6 offenders to $42, raised the jail reimbursement line to $45 million and then $41 million a year, and moved to direct reimbursement with costs submitted within 60 days; Sheriffs' Association executive director Stephen Luce called the rate better than nothing, citing an association study that put the average cost at about $74 per inmate per day [7].
July 2025: The Department of Correction planned to begin paying about $12.7 million owed to county jails for housing state offenders [7].

July 2025: House Enrolled Act 1393 took effect, requiring jails to alert federal immigration authorities, with the county sheriff passing the information to federal officials, after felony or misdemeanor arrests when there is probable cause the person lacks legal status [9].

July 2026: Senate Bill 76 took effect, requiring sheriff's offices and police departments to notify the bail judge when they hold a person subject to an immigration detainer and barring local policies that restrict cooperation with federal officials; St. Joseph County Sheriff Bill Redman said his county already cooperates with ICE, while South Bend Mayor James Mueller said the city will protect the constitutional rights of everyone living there [10].

January 2026: The Sheriffs' Association's 2026 president, Porter County Sheriff Jeffrey Balon, listed jail overcrowding, staffing shortages, the drug epidemic and mental illness among the issues sheriffs raise with legislators [3].

November 2026: Public Question 1 asks voters whether courts may deny bail, for offenses other than murder or treason, when the state proves by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions will reasonably protect others or the community [15]; Sen. Eric Koch (R-Bedford) said releasing some defendants before trial is too dangerous, while Zach Stock of the Indiana Public Defender Council raised concerns about jail overcrowding [13].

incumbent.name: Derek Fell
incumbent.summary: Derek Fell, a Democrat, was selected by party caucus and sworn in as Vigo County sheriff in August 2024 after the death of Sheriff John Plasse; he previously served as the office's chief of operations and is seeking his first full elected term [16, 17, 18].
record: August 2024: Chosen at a Democratic caucus as the only candidate for the vacancy left by Sheriff Plasse's death; at the time he said he did not anticipate 'making any major significant changes' [17, 16].

January 2025: Announced that, with two deputies obtained through a federal grant and additional positions approved by the county council in 2024, patrol staffing would reach 29 deputies once new hires finished training in 2025, compared with 23 to 24 six years earlier; he said the goals were more visible presence, shorter response times, higher minimum patrol staffing and officer safety [19].
January 2025: Began the regular five-year patrol-vehicle replacement cycle and announced a change in patrol uniform colors [19].
May 2025: Announced his 2026 candidacy, naming community engagement, public safety, law enforcement and jail programs as priorities [16].
May 5, 2026: Won the Democratic primary with 48.98% of the vote over Deputy David C. Ewing (28.06%) and Larry Cheeks, Jr. (22.95%) in unofficial results [20].

race_context: Vigo County (Terre Haute) has had an appointed sheriff since August 2024, when Derek Fell was chosen by Democratic caucus after Sheriff John Plasse died; Fell is seeking election in his own right [17, 18].
Democratic primary (May 5, 2026, unofficial): Fell 3,978 votes (48.98%), David C. Ewing 2,279 (28.06%), Larry Cheeks, Jr. 1,864 (22.95%) [20].
Republican primary (May 5, 2026, unofficial): Steve (Top Guns) Ellis 4,537 votes (57.39%), Brad Newman 3,369 (42.61%) [20].
During the primary, other candidates raised issues including jail overcrowding and re-entry programs (Ewing), and the jail's maintenance costs, court security and road coverage (Newman) [21, 22].

A primary candidate forum for sheriff candidates was scheduled for March 11, 2026, at the Vigo County Public Library [23]. No general-election forum or debate between Fell and Ellis was found in available coverage.

Key difference in available coverage: Fell emphasizes continuity and expanded patrol staffing built inside the office; Ellis, a sitting county councilman, emphasizes lowering county spending [19, 24].

candidates.summary: Derek Fell has been Vigo County sheriff since August 2024 after more than two decades with the sheriff's office, most recently as chief of operations [16, 25].
background: Sheriff of Vigo County since August 2024; previously the office's chief of operations [16].
Reported 24 years with the sheriff's office in an April 2026 Tribune-Star candidate questionnaire, with assignments in corrections, patrol, investigations and administration [25].
path_to_ballot: Won the May 5, 2026 Democratic primary with 48.98% of the vote in a three-way race [20].

items: Has pointed to the increase in patrol staffing to 29 deputies, which he called the 'most in known history,' as a way to raise minimum staffing and improve officer safety [19].
Said added deputies are meant to provide more visible presence and reduce some response times [19].
Listed jail programs among his campaign priorities [16].

on_incumbent: Is the current officeholder. When announcing his campaign he described success as 'a team effort'; no statements about Ellis were found [16].
plans: Continue community engagement, public safety and jail programs, per his May 2025 announcement [16].
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or campaign-finance totals were found in available coverage.
gaps: No campaign website or detailed platform was found; coverage of his specific plans for the jail, budget and drug enforcement is limited.
The Tribune-Star questionnaire text was encoded on the page; only his background details were used here.
Search snippets referred to a federal court case over jail staffing under the prior sheriff; this was not read in full and its status is unverified.

candidates.summary: Steve Ellis is a Vigo County councilman and the owner of the Top Guns store in Terre Haute, with nearly 17 years as a special deputy for the county [24, 18].
background: Owner/CEO of the Top Guns store in Terre Haute [24, 18].
Member of the Vigo County Council [24, 18].
Nearly 17 years in law enforcement, including service as a special deputy for Vigo County; has also worked at the county jail and as an emergency medical dispatcher [24].
path_to_ballot: Announced in summer 2025 that he would run on the Republican ballot [26, 18].
Won the May 5, 2026 Republican primary over Terre Haute Police Sgt. Brad Newman, 57.39% to 42.61%, in unofficial results [20].

items: Said he would look for ways to lower county taxes while making sure the department can keep the county safe: 'To represent the taxpayer as best as possible, we have to lower spending' [24].
Says his business experience and council service give him insight into how the county spends money [24].

on_incumbent: No statements by Ellis about Sheriff Fell's record were found in available coverage.
plans: Reduce county spending while maintaining public safety [24].
endorsements_finance: Said he would not accept campaign donations [26].
gaps: No campaign website, questionnaire or forum statements were found; positions on jail operations, staffing, drugs, school safety and immigration enforcement were not found.
His votes on sheriff's office budget items as a county councilman were not reviewed.
Whether his council seat is at-large or district was seen only in a search snippet (at-large) and is unverified.
